rationale: A wins because it separates the real stories instead of stapling them together: "Anker says its home battery needs no major rewiring. Installers will decide if that's true." is a genuine trade angle with a built-in verification fight. B has usable bones, but "Anker is betting it can take on Tesla Powerwall without the rewiring" jams the Tesla comparison and install-code story into one launch frame, then sends the founder to `newsjack-detector` even though the launch itself is already the peg.
gaps_in_A: "The company that makes your phone charger wants to run your house" is a sharp hook, but the "trend" label outruns the supplied facts; A admits it needs "evidence that other consumer-electronics brands are making the same move."

"The prevailing belief is that whole-home batteries mean panel work, transfer switches, and an electrician's week" is useful framing, but it is not in the update. Treat it as a verification question, not a proven premise.
"A profitable charger maker bets on a capital-heavy market" is thin without disclosed investment, segment materiality, or warranty exposure. A says so, but it is still the weakest angle in the set.
gaps_in_B: "A profitable public electronics giant is funding its own move into home energy" invents self-funding. Large and profitable does not prove how the launch is financed.

"The reporter can test whether a high-volume consumer-electronics maker changes who the residential battery buyer even is" overclaims buyer expansion. The update gives brand familiarity, not buyer-reach evidence.

"Anker is betting it can take on Tesla Powerwall without the rewiring" collapses two better stories: competitive positioning and installer/code verification. That costs B the strongest distinct angle A found.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is the wrong default. This is a product launch with a live company peg; an external newsjack could sharpen it, but it is not a prerequisite.
